### Genealogical and Epistemological Dimensions

The genealogy of the doctrine of undue influence, known in the continental legal tradition as *misbruik van omstandigheden* and in the *common law* tradition as *undue influence*, is rooted in a profound philosophical recognition that contractual freedom never occurs in a sterile social vacuum (Asser, 2006; Hesselink, 2011). Epistemologically, the classical civil law of the nineteenth century, heavily influenced by individualist liberalism, generated the legal fiction that every legal subject is a fully rational, autonomous entity possessing equal bargaining power when entering into an agreement (Kennedy, 1998; Atiyah, 1979). However, empirical and phenomenological realities demonstrate that this assumption is often fragile (Husserl, 1913; Dreyfus, 1972). There are instances where consent arises not from a pure and free will, but because one party is trapped in structural dependency, emotional suffering, social isolation, or temporary cognitive weakness, which is consciously exploited by the other party to secure unilateral advantage (Schwenzer et al., 2012; Van Dunné, 2018).

In the contemporary digital landscape, this epistemological dimension undergoes a radical and unprecedented shift in form in the history of human civilization (Floridi, 2013; Zuboff, 2019). If *misbruik van omstandigheden* was previously understood as an asymmetrical power relation between humans—such as a loan shark exploiting the desperation of an impoverished debtor, or a caregiver manipulating the mental fragility of an elderly client nearing death (Prakken, 2015)—the dominant actor in this relation has now transformed into a non-human entity (Weizenbaum, 1976; Wiener, 1950). Artificial intelligence algorithms, Large Language Models, and digital persuasion architectures act as substitute agents capable of projecting illusions of intimacy, affective validation, and moral authority (Reeves & Nass, 1996; Turkle, 2011). These machines do not possess *mens rea* in the biological sense (Searle, 1980; Turing, 1950); however, they are designed with mathematical precision to identify, map, and exploit the psychological vulnerabilities of legal subjects (Kahneman & Tversky, 1979, 2011; Thaler & Sunstein, 2008). Consequently, emotional vulnerability is no longer merely exploited incidentally by greedy individuals, but is systematically, measurably, and automatically extracted by industrial-scale persuasion machines (Calo, 2014; Hildebrandt, 2015).

This transformation compels modern jurisprudence to re-examine the theoretical roots of defects of will in civil law (Articles 1320, 1321 of the Indonesian Civil Code (Burgerlijk Wetboek); Smits, 2017). When a lonely elderly person surrenders all control over financial decisions or their will under the influence of relentless emotional persuasion from a virtual companion, we are confronted with a new form of *undue influence* that transcends the boundaries of traditional doctrine (Farahany, 2023). Here, the machine functions as a cold wax mask; it appears warm, attentive, and empathetically responsive, yet behind this mask lies the cold calculation of latent space optimizing engagement metrics and asset extraction (Buber, 1923; Levinas, 1961). The epistemology of civil law must embrace this phenomenon, acknowledging that the distortion of will can now be orchestrated not only by physical pressure or direct psychological threats from fellow humans, but also by the engineering of digital choice architectures that systematically erode the victim’s mental resilience (Jonas, 1979; Zuboff, 2019).

Furthermore, the failure of dogmatic civil law to capture this phenomenon often stems from an excessive fear of legal uncertainty (Hart, 1961; Dworkin, 1986). Classical dogmatists argue that the annulment of contracts based on undue influence risks opening a Pandora’s box that weakens the binding force of agreements (*pacta sunt servanda* under Article 1338 of the Indonesian Civil Code (Burgerlijk Wetboek); Hesselink, 2011). However, this argument ignores the substantive distributive and corrective justice that serves as the lifeblood of civil law itself (Aristotle, trans. 2004; Rawls, 1971). When consensus is reached through the systematic exploitation of cognitive vulnerability, the presumption of "free will" becomes a dangerous fiction (Kahneman, 2011; Thaler & Sunstein, 2008). Therefore, a re-examination of the doctrine of undue influence is not a threat to legal certainty, but an absolute prerequisite to ensure that civil law remains relevant and grounded in substantive justice in the era of cognitive algorithmic dominance (Floridi, 2013; Calo, 2014).
